name: Spline
tagline: Browser-based 3D design tool for building scenes, animations and interactive 3D you can embed on a website.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Spline is not a feature, it is a 3D content creation suite that happens to run in a browser tab. Under the hood there is a real-time WebGL renderer, a scene graph with a undo-safe editing model, transform gizmos, PBR materials, lighting, physics, an animation and state machine system, event handling, and export pipelines to React, vanilla JS, glTF and video. An agent can absolutely give you a Three.js scene editor in a session, and it will be genuinely useful for placing cubes and tweaking materials. It will not give you the asset library, the animation timeline, the multiplayer editing, or the thousands of small interaction decisions that make Spline feel like a design tool instead of a demo. The gap here is not architecture, it is years of accumulated polish in a domain where polish is the entire product.
coreLoopDIY: A local Three.js scene editor where you add primitives and imported models, move them with gizmos, tweak materials and lights, save the scene as JSON, and export glTF plus a self-contained embeddable viewer.
requirements: Basic comfort with 3D concepts: transforms, materials, lights
whatYouLose: The animation and state machine system, including interaction events and scroll/hover triggers
Asset and template libraries, plus the community scene gallery to remix from
Hosted embeds and the official React/JS runtime that keeps file sizes sane
Physics, particles, and the long tail of material effects you did not know you wanted
moatNotes: The renderer is the commodity part. The editor UX, the asset library and the export runtime are the product.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because designers want to ship a spinning 3D thing on a landing page by Thursday, not maintain a scene editor. Spline collapses modeling, materials, animation, interaction logic and web export into one tool that a non-engineer can actually drive, and then hands back an embed snippet that works. Even people who could wire up Three.js by hand often pay anyway, because the hand-wiring is where the afternoon goes.
notes: A scene editor is a weekend; a design tool is not. The moat is years of interaction polish plus an asset library and an export runtime that nobody wants to rebuild.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user 3D scene editor that runs entirely in the browser with no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- three.js via @react-three/fiber and @react-three/drei
- zustand for the scene store
- leva for the property panels
- No backend. Everything lives in the browser and on disk.

In scope:
- A viewport with orbit controls, a grid, and a default three-point lighting setup.
- Add primitives: box, sphere, plane, cylinder, torus, plus an empty group.
- Import local .glb/.gltf files via drag and drop onto the viewport.
- A hierarchy panel on the left showing the scene graph with select, rename, reparent by drag, duplicate, delete.
- Selection shows drei TransformControls with keyboard shortcuts: W translate, E rotate, R scale, and a toggle for world vs local space.
- A properties panel on the right for the selected object: position, rotation, scale, visibility, and for meshes a MeshStandardMaterial editor with color, roughness, metalness, emissive, opacity.
- Light objects: directional, point, ambient, each with color and intensity controls.
- Environment settings: background color or an HDRI preset from drei, plus shadow toggle.
- Undo/redo for every mutation, implemented as a command stack in the store, bound to Cmd/Ctrl+Z and Shift+Cmd/Ctrl+Z.
- Save and load the scene as a .scene.json file via the File System Access API, with a localStorage autosave fallback.
- Export: glTF binary via GLTFExporter, and a PNG screenshot of the current viewport.
- Export an embeddable viewer: write out a standalone index.html that loads the exported .glb with three.js from a CDN, orbit controls, and the saved camera position. Put it in a downloadable zip via jszip.

Out of scope, do not build these:
- Animation timeline, state machines, interaction events, physics, particles.
- Multiplayer, comments, sharing links, any server.
- Mesh editing or sculpting. Objects are primitives or imported assets only.

Quality bar: 60fps with 200 objects, keyboard shortcuts documented in a help overlay, and a README that explains the scene JSON format. Ship with three example scenes checked into the repo.
